items.explanation: The Cold War ended through Reagan's pressure, Soviet economic rot, and superpower diplomacy — not because American arms makers wanted peace; they profited from the standoff.
options: A. Reagan's military buildup
B. Arms makers' desire to end the arms race
C. The weakness of the Soviet economy
D. Reagan and Bush's Cold War rhetoric
items.stem: All of the following helped end the Cold War EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Reagan's military buildup really did help end the Cold War — it pressured the Soviet economy and forced the arms race to a head. This was a real factor, not the exception.
option_explanations.B: Correct — this is the exception. American arms makers did not want to end the arms race — they profited from it. The Cold War ended through pressure, Soviet weakness, and diplomacy, not because weapons manufacturers wanted peace.
option_explanations.C: The weakness of the Soviet economy really did help end the Cold War — economic rot made the arms race unsustainable. This was a real factor, not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Reagan and Bush's Cold War rhetoric and diplomacy really did help — pressure plus negotiation. This was a real factor, not the exception.

items.explanation: Clinton survived scandal, kept Black voters loyal, and stole GOP issues — but the New Right loathed him; winning them over was the one thing he never did.
options: A. His ability to win over the New Right
B. His support in the Black community
C. His talent for co-opting Republican positions
D. His ability to survive scandal
items.stem: Clinton was a formidable opponent for Republicans for all of the following EXCEPT

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the exception. Clinton never won over the New Right — it loathed him, from the 1994 Republican Revolution to impeachment. Winning them over was the one thing he never did.
option_explanations.B: Clinton's support in the Black community really did make him formidable — he kept Black voters loyal through two terms. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.C: Clinton's talent for co-opting Republican positions really did make him formidable — welfare reform, balanced budgets, crime bills. This is not the exception.
option_explanations.D: Clinton's ability to survive scandal really did make him formidable — he weathered scandals that would have sunk other presidents. This is not the exception.

items.explanation: Greenspan's 1996 remarks show a central banker pulled in two directions — celebrating low, stable inflation while worrying aloud that markets might be overheating — without committing the Fed to any action. They are a window into the Fed's thinking, not proof of a decided policy.

option_explanations.A: Greenspan asked questions; he announced no decision. The Fed never adopted a policy of targeting asset prices, so the remarks cannot prove the Fed had decided to keep raising rates until stocks fell.
option_explanations.B: Carefully worded public remarks are still usable evidence — historians judge what a statement reveals about the speaker's concerns. Dismissing every public statement by an official as worthless would leave most policymaking history blank.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Greenspan is visibly weighing two facts — sustained low inflation was working, yet markets might be overheating — while committing to nothing. The remarks reveal the Fed's dilemma, not a decided policy.
option_explanations.D: The passage says the opposite: Greenspan credited sustained low inflation with reducing uncertainty and risk premiums. He worried that inflation's success sat alongside possible market excess — not that inflation had already returned.

options: A. the remarks prove the Fed had already decided to raise interest rates again and again until stock prices finally fell
B. the remarks are worthless as evidence, because public statements by central bankers never reveal what they really think
C. the remarks reveal a chairman weighing low, stable inflation against overheating markets — without committing to action
D. the remarks show Greenspan believed inflation had already returned to dangerous levels by 1996
items.stem: A historian using Greenspan's 1996 remarks as evidence about Federal Reserve policymaking should recognize that
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan asked in 1996 where to draw the line on which prices matter — noting that sustained low inflation reduces uncertainty and risk premiums, but warning that markets might be gripped by 'irrational exuberance.'
—After Alan Greenspan's remarks, December 1996

items.explanation: The dot-com mania Greenspan named in 1996 peaked in March 2000 and then collapsed -- the NASDAQ lost nearly four-fifths of its value by 2002. The 2008 crisis was a housing bubble, 1987 a one-day crash, and the Depression a different era entirely.
options: A. The Great Depression
B. The stock market crash of 1987
C. The dot-com crash of 2000-2001
D. The financial crisis of 2008
items.stem: The 'irrational exuberance' Greenspan warned about ended with
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan asked in 1996 where to draw the line on which prices matter — noting that sustained low inflation reduces uncertainty and risk premiums, but warning that markets might be gripped by 'irrational exuberance.'
—After Alan Greenspan's remarks, December 1996

option_explanations.A: The Great Depression belonged to a different era — the 1930s, sixty years before Greenspan's 1996 warning. The 'irrational exuberance' episode was the 1990s stock mania.
option_explanations.B: The 1987 crash was a one-day crash, not the end of the 1990s mania — Greenspan spoke in 1996, nine years after 1987, about the bubble then building.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The dot-com mania Greenspan named in 1996 peaked in March 2000 and then collapsed — the NASDAQ lost nearly four-fifths of its value by 2002.
option_explanations.D: The 2008 financial crisis was a housing bubble, not the stock mania Greenspan named in 1996. The 'irrational exuberance' bubble was the dot-com crash.

items.explanation: In 1928-29 the Federal Reserve watched speculation mount and acted timidly and too late -- the lesson Greenspan was determined not to repeat. His 1996 warning was the 1929 failure in reverse: a central banker publicly fretting about asset prices before the crash. The 1930s Fed contracted credit, the 1940s Fed pegged rates for war finance, and the 2010s Fed moved slowly, not rapidly.
options: A. World War II, when the Fed pegged interest rates to finance the war
B. The late 1920s, when the Fed did little to restrain stock speculation
C. The early 1930s, when the Fed aggressively expanded credit
D. The 2010s, when the Fed raised interest rates rapidly
items.stem: Greenspan's public worry about asset bubbles most directly contrasts with the Federal Reserve's stance in
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt (paraphrased).

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan asked in 1996 where to draw the line on which prices matter — noting that sustained low inflation reduces uncertainty and risk premiums, but warning that markets might be gripped by 'irrational exuberance.'
—After Alan Greenspan's remarks, December 1996

option_explanations.A: During World War II the Fed pegged interest rates to finance the war — a policy of accommodation for war finance, not a stance on asset bubbles. It is not the contrast Greenspan's warning draws.
option_explanations.B: Correct. In 1928–29 the Federal Reserve watched speculation mount and acted timidly and too late. Greenspan's 1996 public worry about asset prices was the 1929 failure in reverse — a central banker fretting about a bubble before the crash.
option_explanations.C: The early-1930s Fed contracted credit, worsening the Depression — it did not aggressively expand it. And its stance was not about worrying over bubbles; the question asks for the contrast with Greenspan's bubble-worry.
option_explanations.D: The 2010s Fed raised rates slowly and gradually, not rapidly — and its stance was not the 'watch speculation and do little' failure of 1929. The direct contrast is the late 1920s.
